before.content_html:
Growing Up & Change

Growing up is not a single moment — it is a series of small shocks. The Youth and Age anthology contains several poems in which a child or young person stands at the edge of experience, half-aware that something is shifting. The poets capture the exact texture of that threshold: the dawning consciousness of mortality, the loneliness of moving into the unknown, and the quiet alarm of understanding more than you can yet name.

Key Fact

Three poems that deal most directly with the experience of growing up are Hopkins’s Spring and Fall (a child weeping over falling leaves), Hardy’s Midnight on the Great Western (a boy travelling alone into the unknown), and Komunyakaa’s Venus’s-flytraps (a five-year-old narrator at the edge of adult knowledge). Each uses a young subject to explore how growing up involves confronting things we cannot yet fully understand.

Hopkins: Spring and Fall

Hopkins addresses his poem directly to a child called Margaret, who is crying at the sight of autumn leaves falling. His opening question — “Margaret, are you grieving / Over Goldengrove unleaving?” — seems to mock her gently, but the poem quickly turns serious. Hopkins suggests that the child’s grief is instinctive and profound: she cannot yet name what she is mourning, but some part of her already knows.

The poem’s central insight is that grief for the world — for decay, for loss, for the passing of beautiful things — is ultimately grief for oneself. Hopkins writes: “It is the blight man was born for, / It is Margaret you mourn for.” The child weeping over dead leaves is, without knowing it, mourning her own mortality. This is the defining feature of growing up in Hopkins’s view: the dawning realisation that you, too, will decay. The invented compound “Goldengrove” and the neologisms “wanwood leafmeal” are characteristic of Hopkins: dense, compressed language that makes the familiar feel strange and weighty.

The adult speaker’s prediction is bleak: growing up means growing colder to nature’s losses. The child weeps precisely because she has not yet built emotional defences. “Colder” implies both emotional numbness and a kind of death — the warmth of childhood sensitivity will eventually be replaced by adult indifference. Hopkins uses the word “blight” to suggest that this coldness is not just natural but a kind of corruption, a flaw —“the blight man was born for.” Growing up, in this poem, is inseparable from a loss of feeling as well as a loss of innocence.

Hardy: Midnight on the Great Western

Hardy’s poem observes a boy travelling alone on a night train, described throughout as “the journeying boy.” The phrase recurs as a refrain in each stanza, and its deliberate vagueness is part of the poem’s power: Hardy gives the boy no name, no known origin, no destination. He is simply a child in transit, “Bewrapt past knowing to what he was going, / Or whence he came.”

The boy wears a key around his neck on a string, and has a ticket in his hat-band. These are the only signs of identity or belonging he carries. Hardy is struck by the boy’s apparent calm: “calmly, as if incurious quite / On all at stake.” The phrase “all at stake” hints at how enormous this transition is — the boy is moving from one world to another — yet he shows no fear. Hardy finds this composure almost otherworldly, asking whether the boy possesses a “sphere” of understanding far above the adult world, a vantage point from which life’s griefs seem small. The image of the refrain “journeying boy” fixes him in perpetual motion, as if growing up itself is simply a journey with no fixed end.

Key Fact

Hardy’s boy carries a key on a string around his neck and a ticket in his hat-band. The key represents a home or destination he belongs to; the ticket grants permission to travel. Together they suggest that this child exists at a crossing point: between the old world and the new one, between belonging and being adrift.

Komunyakaa: Venus’s-flytraps

Komunyakaa’s poem is narrated by a five-year-old child in the American South, and uses the child’s innocent observations to expose a world of danger, poverty, and adult violence. The child opens with bravado — “Don’t mess with me / ’Cause I have my Lone Ranger / Six-shooter” — but the poem quickly reveals the dramatic irony of that confidence: the child is five, and the world around them is far more threatening than any toy gun.

The child’s growing awareness surfaces in glimpsed fragments: they have seen “What a train did to a cow” (a line the child recounts as casually as any other observation), they hear “people / Telling each other secrets” from under the house, and crucially, their own mother’s words pierce the poem near its end: “My mama says I’m a mistake. / That I made her a bad girl.” This line arrives with devastating quiet. The child does not know how to process it; the poem does not explain it. This is how Komunyakaa captures the experience of growing up: things known before they can be understood, truths absorbed before the child has the vocabulary or context to make sense of them. The poem ends with the child’s imagination expanding outward: “These yellow flowers / Go on forever. / Almost to Detroit. / Almost to the sea.”

Similarity: Both poems present a child navigating a world they do not fully understand. Hardy’s boy is physically in transit; Komunyakaa’s child is psychologically in transit — absorbing experiences and knowledge that exceed their years.

Difference: Hardy observes his subject from the outside, with adult sympathy and wonder. Komunyakaa lets the child speak, creating unreliable narration in which the reader understands more than the narrator does. Hardy’s tone is melancholy and compassionate; Komunyakaa’s is unsettling because the child’s cheerful voice sits against genuinely dark material.

Form: Hardy uses regular four-line stanzas with a refrain, giving the poem a controlled, almost ballad-like quality. Komunyakaa uses irregular spacing and fragmented lines that mime the child’s scattered, associative thinking — the form enacts growing consciousness.

Sheers: Farther

Sheers’s poem is narrated by a parent climbing a mountain with their ageing father. The title contains a pun: “farther” means both a greater distance and a father. The poem captures the moment when the parent realises the generational tipping point has been reached: “again I felt the tipping in the scales of us, / the intersection of our ages.” The child has become the stronger one; the parent is ageing; the roles are beginning to reverse.

Growing up, in Sheers’s poem, is something you only fully recognise by looking at someone older. The son has grown; he knows it only when he sees his father’s “bent head” and hears his “breath reaching me, short and sharp and solitary.” The poem ends with tender hope: “with every step apart, I’m another closer to you.” Change and distance do not mean loss — they can bring a different kind of closeness.
before.exam_tip_html: When comparing growing-up poems, avoid saying a poem is simply “sad” or “hopeful.” Instead, identify the specific method the poet uses to convey the moment of change — a refrain, a dramatic revelation, a direct address, a shift in perspective — and explain its effect. For 40-mark comparison questions, your second poem should genuinely extend or challenge the argument of your first, not simply repeat it with different evidence.

knowledge_checks.q: In 'Spring and Fall', what does Hopkins say the child is ultimately mourning?
In 'Midnight on the Great Western', what two objects identify the journeying boy?
options: A ticket in his hat and a key on a string

knowledge_checks.q: Hopkins writes that as the heart grows older, it will come to such sights _____.
In 'Farther', Sheers describes feeling 'the _____ in the scales of us' as he looks back at his ageing father.
Match each poem to the method used to present the growing-up experience:
right: Refrain repeating the boy's name to suggest perpetual transition
Direct address to a child to reveal she mourns her own mortality
Child narrator whose innocent voice contrasts with disturbing adult knowledge

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Hopkins uses language to present a child’s first encounter with loss in ‘Spring and Fall’.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated, sustained analysis of specific language choices (e.g. neologisms, direct address, the final couplet) with precise terminology and a clear argument about what Hopkins suggests growing up involves. Secure: Clear analysis of two or more language features with explanation of effect linked to theme of growing up and change. Developing: Some identification of features with limited explanation; response may be feature-spotted rather than argued. Emerging: Simple points about the poem with little or no use of evidence.

practice_questions.text: How does Hardy use the figure of the ‘journeying boy’ to explore the experience of transition in ‘Midnight on the Great Western’?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores the refrain as a structural device, the symbolic objects (key, ticket), and Hardy’s use of rhetorical questions to convey the speaker’s wonder; clear argument about what the poem suggests about growing up alone. Secure: Analysis of at least two techniques with effect linked to theme of transition and the unknown. Developing: Describes what happens rather than analysing how language creates meaning; limited quotation. Emerging: Very general comments on the poem with no close reading.

practice_questions.text: Compare how two poets from the Youth and Age collection present a child’s growing awareness of the adult world. [40 marks]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Structured, two-poem comparison with a sustained argument; perceptive analysis of language, form, and structure in both poems; exploration of how context shapes meaning; methods compared as well as themes. Secure: Clear comparison of two poems with relevant evidence and explanation; some analysis of methods; argument maintained throughout. Developing: Some comparative points but may drift into describing each poem separately; evidence used but not always analysed closely. Emerging: Basic comments on two poems with little comparison or analysis.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Komunyakaa uses the child’s voice to create dramatic irony in ‘Venus’s-flytraps’.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Perceptive analysis of the gap between what the child narrator understands and what the reader perceives; explores specific moments of dark revelation (the mother’s words, the train, the secrets) and how the child’s tone contrasts with the disturbing content. Secure: Clear analysis of dramatic irony with at least two examples and explanation of effect. Developing: Identifies the child’s limited understanding but does not analyse how language creates the irony. Emerging: Simple retelling of what the child says with minimal analysis.

practice_questions.text: How does Sheers present the relationship between growing up and growing apart in ‘Farther’?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analysis of the title’s pun, the tipping-point imagery, the physical details of the climb, and the paradox of the final lines; sustained argument about what the poem suggests about how growing up reshapes family relationships. Secure: Clear analysis of two or more techniques with effect linked to the theme of generational change. Developing: Some relevant points but limited analysis; may focus on paraphrase rather than close reading. Emerging: Very general comments with little reference to specific language.

practice_questions.text: Compare how two poets in the Youth and Age collection use form and structure to reflect the experience of growing up. [40 marks]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated comparison of form and structure across two poems, with clear argument about how formal choices (refrain, fragmentation, irregular spacing, regular stanzas) enact the theme of change; both poems analysed with precision. Secure: Clear comparison of form and structure in two poems; relevant evidence and explanation; some exploration of how form supports meaning. Developing: Identifies structural features in both poems but treats them separately rather than comparatively; explanation of effect is limited. Emerging: Basic identification of form with little analysis.

before.content_html:
The Poetry Exam: What You’re Being Asked to Do

In your poetry exam you answer one question split into two parts. Part (a) asks you to compare a named poem from the cluster with an unseen poem: you must analyse both poems and explore what they share and how they differ. Part (b) asks you to write about a different poem from the cluster of your own choice, focusing on a related idea or theme. Strong students plan their poem choices before they enter the exam room.

The examiners reward four things: a personal, critical response to the poems; analysis of language, form and structure; awareness of context; and — especially in part (a) — sustained comparative writing. These are the four assessment objectives (AOs), and every mark you earn connects to at least one of them.

Key Fact

Part (a) is a comparison of a named cluster poem with an unseen poem. Part (b) is an independent question on a different cluster poem of your choice. You should prepare your part (b) poem selection in advance, but stay flexible — read the question first and pick the poem that fits best.

A Framework for Comparison

A reliable comparison framework covers three layers: poetic methods, themes, and contexts. Work through them in your planning, then weave them together in your paragraphs rather than separating them into three distinct blocks.

For every quotation you use, ask three questions: What technique is being used? What does it make the reader feel or think? Why did the poet make this choice? Common techniques to track across the cluster include imagery (especially nature imagery used to represent lost childhood or approaching death), apostrophe (direct address to a person or place), form and structure (does the poem fragment or remain tightly controlled?), and voice (is the speaker a child, a parent, or an observer?). When comparing, choose a technique that both poems share and show how each poet uses it differently.

The cluster’s central themes are: the innocence of childhood and its inevitable loss; mortality, time and the approach of death; the relationship between generations (parent and child, old and young); memory as unreliable or painful; and the vulnerability of the very young. When comparing, identify which theme connects the two poems most strongly and build your essay around it.

Context in this cluster means the biographical moment of the poet (Keats writing under the shadow of tuberculosis; Frost writing after a real farm accident; Blake writing in an era when child labour was widespread) and broader literary contexts (the Romantic idealisation of childhood; Victorian attitudes to death; modern confessional poetry). A single, well-integrated contextual sentence per paragraph is more effective than a lengthy biographical paragraph that ignores the poem.

Quotation Bank: Eight Key Quotations

Every quotation below has been taken verbatim from the canonical cluster poems. Use these in the exam embedded in analytical sentences — never as block quotations dropped in without comment.

Key Fact

For each quotation below: learn the poet and poem, a single key technique, and the thematic link to at least one other cluster poem. That is the minimum required for a full comparative paragraph in part (a).

1. “It is Margaret you mourn for.” — Hopkins, Spring and Fall. The volta-like final line turns the whole poem on its head: the child Margaret, who weeps at falling leaves, is unconsciously grieving her own future death. The use of the second person (“you”) makes the priest-speaker’s insight feel both intimate and inevitable. Compare with Brontë’s The Bluebell, where an adult speaker similarly finds that an object of natural beauty triggers grief for lost childhood.

2. “O, that lone flower recalled to me / My happy childhood’s hours / When bluebells seemed like fairy gifts / A prize among the flowers.” — Brontë, The Bluebell. The symbol of the single bluebell condenses an entire lost world into a visual image. The adjective “lone” mirrors the speaker’s isolation, while “fairy gifts” suggests childhood’s magical thinking has been replaced by an adult consciousness that can no longer sustain it.

3. “Bewrapt past knowing to what he was going, / Or whence he came.” — Hardy, Midnight on the Great Western. The invented word “Bewrapt” (wrapped in a stupor) suggests the child is neither fully conscious nor able to comprehend his journey. Hardy presents childhood as a state of unknowing, suspended between past and future — a contrast to Hopkins’s suggestion that children feel more than they can articulate.

4. “All lost things lie under closing water / in that lake with the poor man’s daughter.” — Clarke, Cold Knap Lake. This closing couplet turns personal memory into something universal: childhood, near-death, and the past itself are all submerged and unreachable. The apostrophe-like ending collapses the specific event into myth. Clarke’s question earlier (“Was I there?”) makes memory itself unreliable, a theme also present in Brontë’s nostalgic looking-back.

Selecting Quotations Under Exam Pressure

In the exam you will not have the texts in front of you, so short, embedded quotations are safer than long ones you might misremember. A single striking word or short phrase (“Bewrapt”, “gleaned”, “intersection”) is often more analytical than a three-line block. If you cannot remember the exact wording, paraphrase with a brief signal: “Hardy describes the child as caught between worlds” — then add the closest line you can recall.

When choosing your part (b) poem, select one you know well and one that connects clearly to the part (a) theme. For example, if part (a) names Spring and Fall (loss of innocence), strong part (b) choices include The Bluebell (adult loss of childhood) or Cold Knap Lake (unreliable memory of childhood). Avoid choosing a poem just because you like it — the connection to the question matters most.

Worked Example Paragraphs

Example 1 — Comparing mortality in Keats and Frost (part a style):

Both poets present youth as tragically cut short, but while Keats focuses on the speaker’s fear of unfulfilled potential (“Before my pen has glean’d my teeming brain”), Frost denies his subject even that self-awareness — the boy dies and the community simply “turned to their affairs.” The agricultural metaphor of gleaning in Keats implies richness that will be wasted; Frost’s bleak declarative syntax implies that in a working farm community, death is simply the end of a task. Both use brevity to devastating effect: Keats compresses a lifetime’s ambition into a single noun (“teeming brain”), Frost compresses a life’s end into a half-line (“Little — less — nothing!”).

Example 2 — Analysing the parent–child relationship in Sheers (part b style):

In Farther, Owen Sheers uses the walk up Skirrid mountain as a extended metaphor for the passage of time between father and son. When the speaker notes “the tipping in the scales of us, / the intersection of our ages,” the precision of “intersection” — a mathematical term for the point where two lines cross — suggests a moment that cannot last, a brief equilibrium before the balance shifts irreversibly. The poem’s closing paradox — “with every step apart, I’m another closer to you” — redefines distance itself: physical separation is also a form of approach, because the son is walking the same path his father has already walked.

Example 3 — Analysing the moment of loss in Cold Knap Lake (part b style):

Clarke’s final couplet — “All lost things lie under closing water / in that lake with the poor man’s daughter” — transforms a specific near-drowning into a symbol of everything childhood buries. The generalisation “All lost things” is earned by the poem’s earlier accumulation of detail: the child’s wet dress, the mother’s heroism, the father’s violent punishment. The word “closing” makes memory feel active — it is not simply still water but water that is sealing over, refusing to give back what it has taken. This connects directly to the poem’s earlier destabilisation of memory itself (“Was I there?”), suggesting that all versions of the past are eventually sealed off from the present self.

practice_questions.text:
Compare how Hopkins in 'Spring and Fall' and a poem of your choice from the Youth and Age cluster present the idea that children feel more than they understand.

You should write about:
- the methods each poet uses to explore this idea
- any relevant contexts
- your own informed personal response
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Perceptive, sustained comparison; precise analysis of Hopkins's closing turn ('It is Margaret you mourn for') and a well-chosen second poem; technique, effect and meaning chained in every paragraph; contextual comment fully integrated into analysis.
Secure: Clear comparison with relevant quotation from both poems; some analysis of technique; context mentioned.
Developing: Identifies theme in both poems; quotation present but analysis mainly paraphrase.
Emerging: Describes both poems without comparison or close language analysis.

practice_questions.text:
Plan a comparative response to the following question: 'Compare how poets present the moment when childhood ends.'

Your plan should identify:
- which two cluster poems you would use and why
- two key quotations from each poem
- the comparative point each paragraph would make
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Thoughtful poem choices justified by thematic fit; quotations are specific and verbatim; paragraph plans make genuine comparative points rather than summaries.
Secure: Reasonable poem choices; quotations identified; paragraph intentions stated.
Developing: Poem choices made but justification thin; quotations approximate or paraphrased.
Emerging: Poems named but no clear planning structure.

practice_questions.text:
Write a full analytical paragraph comparing how Keats in 'When I have fears that I may cease to be' and Frost in 'Out-Out' present the fear of dying young.

Your paragraph should include:
- at least one embedded quotation from each poem
- analysis of a specific technique in each
- a comparative connective to link the two poems
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Technique identified and its effect precisely explained; meaning extended beyond the obvious; comparative connective used to create a sustained analytical thread rather than two mini-essays.
Secure: Technique named and quotation embedded; some effect explained; comparison attempted.
Developing: Quotation present but technique label replaces analysis.
Emerging: Paraphrase of both poems with little comparison.

practice_questions.text:
How does Clarke in 'Cold Knap Lake' present memory as unreliable or incomplete?

In your answer you should write about:
- Clarke's use of language and structure
- your own informed personal response
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Perceptive reading of the rhetorical question ('Was I there?') as structural pivot; tracks imagery of water and obscured vision through the poem; personal response is argued, not merely stated.
Secure: Clear analysis of the question and closing couplet; some structural comment.
Developing: Identifies that Clarke is uncertain; some quotation but limited method analysis.
Emerging: Retells the poem's events.

practice_questions.text: Choose any two poems from the Youth and Age cluster that present the vulnerability of the very young. Compare how each poet creates a sense of that vulnerability through their choice of language.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Perceptive poem choices (for example, Gunn's 'Baby Song' and Sexton's 'Red Roses', or Plath's 'You're' and Frost's 'Out-Out'); analysis precise and comparative; technique, effect, meaning chained; context woven in.
Secure: Relevant poems chosen; quotations used; some comparative analysis.
Developing: Poems described more than analysed; comparison limited.
Emerging: One poem focused on; little comparison.

practice_questions.text:
'The poets in the Youth and Age cluster suggest that old age and youth are more alike than they are different.'

How far do you agree with this view? Write about at least two poems from the cluster in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated argument — Sheers's 'intersection of our ages' as convergence; Keats's and Hardy's isolated figures as parallel; some poems used to complicate the statement (Frost's sharp division between the boy's death and the adults who survive). Context integrated.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence from two poems; comparison present.
Developing: Agreement or disagreement asserted but evidence limited to one side.
Emerging: Lists themes without constructing an argument.
